To: Engineering Leadership
From: Infrastructure Working Group
Subject: Local AI hardware: expand or optimise?

We are at a decision point on how to serve growing demand for local AI workloads. The options on the table are straightforward: purchase additional hardware to increase raw capacity, or invest engineering effort in improving utilisation of the fleet we already own. This memo lays out the trade-offs and offers a recommendation.

The most obvious argument for buying hardware is that it converts money into capacity quickly. If we have a clear, near-term workload that saturates current resources, additional cards shorten the path to delivery. Yet capital expenditure is a one-way door. Once purchased, the cost is sunk, and the economics of utilisation become fixed. If demand does not materialise as forecast, we are left carrying idle assets, maintenance contracts, and the quiet drag of underused silicon. The upfront price of a system is also a poor proxy for total cost of ownership. Power, cooling, networking, spares, and the engineering time required to integrate and monitor new machines all accumulate over the life of the asset. A cheap purchase can become an expensive liability if those factors are not modelled honestly.

Latency and reliability complicate the picture further. Adding hardware does not automatically improve response times. If our current bottleneck is not compute but rather data movement, model loading, or shared storage, more cards may simply queue behind the same choke points. Reliability, too, is not a function of quantity. A larger fleet increases the surface area for failure, and without mature provisioning, failover, and monitoring, we may trade a small, predictable problem for a larger, less predictable one. We should be wary of the assumption that more hardware is inherently more robust; it is only more robust if the surrounding systems are designed to tolerate failure.

The opportunity cost of a purchase is easy to underestimate. Every dollar and every engineering hour spent on procuring and integrating new hardware is an hour not spent on improving the efficiency of what we have. Optimisation work, such as better scheduling, finer-grained batching, model quantisation, caching of frequent requests, and smarter allocation of shared resources, can yield compounding returns. Unlike a capital purchase, these improvements are not tied to a single point in time; they can be revisited, tuned, and extended as workloads evolve. They also tend to be reversible. If a change turns out to be harmful, we can roll it back, whereas a procurement decision is far harder to unwind without financial loss.

Reversibility is a useful lens for the decision as a whole. A preference for options that preserve future choices is prudent when uncertainty is high. We do not yet have a long enough track record to be confident in our demand forecasts, and the pace of model and tooling change means that today’s hardware choices may be suboptimal in a year. By contrast, improving utilisation is a path that keeps our options open. It reduces the pressure to buy, buys time to gather better data, and positions us to make a more informed capital decision later if it becomes necessary.

Given all of this, our recommendation is to prioritise a focused programme of utilisation improvement before committing to new hardware. We propose dedicating a small, time-boxed effort to measure where our current systems actually spend their time, to eliminate obvious waste, and to implement the highest-impact efficiency measures. This effort should be treated with the same seriousness as a procurement project, with clear goals and a review point.

We acknowledge uncertainty. It is possible that our analysis will reveal a hard capacity ceiling that cannot be addressed through software alone, in which case a targeted hardware purchase may become the right next step. But that conclusion is more credible once we have better data, and it is a conclusion we can reach with greater confidence and less risk if we first exhaust the reversible, lower-cost options available to us. In short, we recommend optimising first, and buying only if the evidence demands it.

To: Engineering Leadership
From: [Your Name]
Subject: Recommendation on AI Hardware: Purchase vs. Utilisation
Date: [Date]

We are at a familiar inflection point. The queue of promising experiments is growing faster than our current compute can comfortably serve, and the question before us is whether to buy more local AI hardware or to improve the utilisation of what we already own. This is not merely a procurement decision; it is a statement about how we value our engineering time, our financial prudence, and our long-term architectural flexibility. After weighing the trade-offs, my recommendation is to prioritise a deep, structured effort to improve utilisation of our existing fleet, while simultaneously scoping a smaller, targeted hardware purchase to address the most acute and predictable bottlenecks.

The most immediate argument for more hardware is the reduction of latency. If our current systems are queuing jobs and causing developers to wait, that friction compounds into lost productivity and a slower feedback loop. However, simply adding more machines does not guarantee that this latency will be evenly distributed or that it will solve the root cause. Often, the bottleneck is not raw compute but memory bandwidth, storage I/O, or a poorly partitioned workload. Throwing hardware at a software-defined problem is a costly and often temporary fix. The financial outlay is significant and immediate, and it commits us to a new asset with its own maintenance, power, and cooling overheads. This is where the concept of opportunity cost becomes stark. Every dollar spent on underutilised silicon is a dollar not spent on a senior engineer’s time, a critical security audit, or a feature that directly generates revenue. The opportunity cost of a poor utilisation strategy is not just the idle hardware; it is the entire spectrum of forgone investment.

Conversely, the path of improving utilisation is more intellectually demanding but far more reversible. It requires us to treat our compute as a shared, precious resource and to instrument it deeply. We need to understand who is using what, when, and why. Are there idle GPUs during the day that are saturated at night? Can we implement smarter scheduling to pack workloads more efficiently? Can we adopt model distillation or quantisation to make our existing models run faster on the same hardware? This work is a direct investment in our engineering culture. It builds internal tooling and expertise that will serve us regardless of what hardware we eventually own. The financial cost is primarily in engineering time, which is a more flexible and ultimately more valuable currency. The reliability of this approach is high; we are not introducing new, untested physical systems into our environment. The risk is low, and the potential upside—a dramatic increase in effective capacity without a corresponding capital expenditure—is enormous.

The question of reversibility is central. A decision to buy hardware is largely irreversible in the short term. We will own this asset, with its specific power and cooling needs, for a depreciation cycle of three to five years. If our workload patterns shift, or if a more efficient cloud provider or a new architectural paradigm emerges, we are left with a potentially stranded asset. Improving utilisation, on the other hand, is a series of reversible, incremental steps. We can implement a new scheduler, test it, and roll it back if it proves problematic. We can refactor a model, measure the improvement, and decide whether to keep it. This optionality is a form of financial and technical resilience. It allows us to learn and adapt without being locked into a rigid physical footprint.

That said, I acknowledge significant uncertainty. Our current monitoring is not granular enough to make a fully data-driven decision. We do not have a precise, real-time map of utilisation by team, project, and model type. There is a risk that a deep dive into utilisation reveals that our hardware is, in fact, already near its practical limits for the workloads we are running, and that a targeted purchase is the only way forward. Furthermore, the lead time for custom hardware can be long, and if we delay a necessary purchase, we may stall a critical project. The uncertainty is not in whether we need to act, but in the precise nature of the action.

Therefore, my recommendation is a hybrid path, sequenced to preserve optionality. For the next four to six weeks, we should form a small, cross-functional task force to conduct a rigorous utilisation audit. Their goal is not to write a report, but to identify and implement at least three concrete improvements—such as dynamic scheduling, right-sizing instances, or adopting more efficient inference runtimes. In parallel, we should identify the single most predictable, long-term workload, such as a training job that is on a critical path, and scope a small, modular hardware purchase to accelerate just that workload. This approach respects the financial discipline of improving what we have, acknowledges the latency needs of our most critical work, and, most importantly, keeps our options open. We are choosing to learn before we commit, and in a domain that changes this quickly, that is the most reliable strategy of all.
